title: Constructors and initialization
summary: Learn how Java constructors create valid objects, how initialization order works, and how to avoid partially initialized or overly flexible objects.

blocks.text: A constructor is the entry point used when a new Java object is created. Its job is not merely to copy arguments into fields: it should establish the minimum valid state that lets the object safely participate in the system.

A constructor has the same name as its class and has no return type. Java invokes it during `new`. If you declare no constructor, Java provides a no-argument default constructor; once you declare a constructor yourself, that implicit default is no longer supplied.

blocks.title: Require essential data

items: Instance fields are first assigned their default values (`0`, `false`, or `null`).
Instance field initializers and instance initializer blocks run in textual order.
For inheritance, superclass construction occurs before the subclass's instance initialization and constructor body.

blocks.title: Constructor chaining
blocks.text: Use `this(...)` to delegate to another constructor in the same class, or `super(...)` to invoke a superclass constructor. The constructor invocation must be the first statement in a Java constructor.

Prefer constructors that require essential dependencies and values. Validate inputs at the boundary. Use `final` for fields that should not be reassigned after initialization. Avoid constructors that perform slow network calls, start background threads or hide complicated workflows; those make object creation difficult to test and reason about.

blocks.title: Constructor validation

blocks.text: Overloaded constructors can offer a small number of clear creation options. When there are many optional parameters or the creation rules have meaningful names, a static factory method can be clearer, for example `Money.zero(USD)` or `User.register(email)`. A factory is an alternative creation API, not a replacement for validation.

items: Leaving required fields null and expecting every caller to remember to set them later.
Publishing setters for values that should never change.
Putting unrelated business workflows or I/O inside a constructor.
Creating many ambiguous overloads with similar parameter types.
Allowing `this` to escape from a constructor before initialization is complete.

blocks.text: Design a `Product` constructor. A product must have a non-blank SKU, a non-blank name and a non-negative price. Decide which fields should be final, write the validation rules in plain language, and then implement the constructor in Java.

questions.prompt: What is the primary responsibility of an initializer or constructor?

options.text: Establish a valid initial state for the object
Perform every workflow the object may ever need
Delay all validation until later method calls

questions.explanation: Construction or initialization should establish the invariants required for the object to be used safely.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of constructor validation?

options.text: Ensure the object starts in a valid state
Delay validation until the object is used

questions.explanation: Validating required data during construction prevents invalid or partially initialized objects from entering the system.

questions.prompt: When is a named factory method useful?

options.text: When it communicates a meaningful or alternate creation path
Whenever a class has any field

questions.explanation: A named factory can make creation intent explicit, but validation is still required.

1.text: A constructor is called when a C++ object is initialized. Its job is not merely to copy arguments into fields: it should establish the minimum valid state that lets the object safely participate in the system.

2.text: A constructor has the same name as its class and has no return type. C++ supports member initializer lists, which initialize members before the constructor body runs. If you declare no constructor, the compiler may generate a default constructor when the rules permit it; declaring constructors changes which implicit constructors are available.

4.title: Require essential data

items: Base-class subobjects are initialized before members of the derived class.
Data members are initialized in the order they are declared in the class, not the order written in the member initializer list.
The constructor body runs after base classes and data members have been initialized.
Destruction happens in reverse order: the destructor body runs, then members and base subobjects are destroyed.

7.title: Member initializer lists
7.text: Prefer member initializer lists for initializing data members. Their order follows the class declaration, so declare members in the order that reflects their dependencies.

10.title: Constructor validation

12.text: A small number of overloaded constructors can offer clear creation options. When creation has meaningful names or many optional choices, use a named factory function such as `Money::zero(USD)` or `User::registerUser(email)`. A factory is an alternative creation API, not a replacement for validation.

implementationNotes.title: Initialization model
implementationNotes.text: C++ initializes members before the constructor body and destroys them in reverse order. Python separates allocation (`__new__`) from initialization (`__init__`). Both languages need explicit validation of required state.

1.text: In Python, creating an instance calls `__new__` to create it and then `__init__` to initialize it. Most application classes customize `__init__`, whose job is to establish the minimum valid state that lets the object safely participate in the system.

2.text: `__init__` is an initializer, not the allocator, and it does not return the new object. It receives `self` plus the arguments passed to the class call. Validate required inputs there. If an object needs a different creation process, a `@classmethod` factory can provide a named alternative.

4.title: Require essential data

items: The class call first creates an instance through `__new__` (normally inherited from `object`).
Python then calls `__init__` on that instance with the supplied arguments.
The initializer assigns attributes and validates the initial state; it should not return a value.
If initialization raises an exception, the class call fails and the partially initialized instance is not returned to the caller.

7.title: Initializer versus factory
7.text: Use `__init__` for ordinary instance initialization. Use a `@classmethod` factory when creation needs a meaningful name or alternate input format, such as `Money.zero("USD")` or `User.register(email)`. Keep network calls and unrelated workflows outside initialization.

10.title: Constructor validation

12.text: A class can provide a small number of alternate constructors with `@classmethod`. Use meaningful names when they make the creation rule clearer, for example `Money.zero("USD")` or `User.register(email)`. A factory is an alternative creation API, not a replacement for validation.

16.text: Design a `Product` initializer. A product must have a non-blank SKU, a non-blank name and a non-negative price. Decide which attributes should be treated as immutable, write the validation rules in plain language, and implement `__init__` or a named `@classmethod` factory where appropriate.

implementationNotes.text: C++ initializes members before the constructor body and destroys them in reverse order. Python separates allocation (`__new__`) from initialization (`__init__`). Both languages need explicit validation of required state.

implementationNotes.title: Java constructor rules
implementationNotes.text: A constructor has the class name and no return type. `this(...)` delegates to another constructor in the same class and must be the first statement. `super(...)` invokes a parent constructor.
